title: Releaf
subtitle: Small actions. A lighter footprint.
summary: An iOS app that brings reuse ideas, carbon tracking, and a sustainability community into everyday life.
intro: Sustainability becomes more approachable when the next step is concrete. I helped build Releaf around the things people already have, the habits they want to change, and a community to share those experiments with.
sections: From information to a daily habit

Releaf brings together ways to reuse everyday materials, estimates of carbon emissions, and a dedicated online community. The aim is to give environmental information a useful place in a person’s routine: an idea to try, an action to record, or something to share.
The system behind the experience

My work included Django backend features for user accounts, Waterdrop rewards, achievements, and notifications. I also developed supporting AI services for image analysis and retrieving sustainability information. These pieces connect the visible app experience to the accounts, content, and feedback that keep it working.
Building with a team

As a cofounder of Rematter Cooperation, I worked across software and the broader project. We raised $2,000 in funding and earned a top-two team placement in the 2025 China High School Social Innovation Competition and Incubation Camp. Releaf reached more than 5,000 downloads.
note: Download and funding figures are reported in my résumé. Carbon estimates are informational; they are not direct measurements of environmental impact.

technical.heading: From a photo to a useful next step.
modules: A shared request contract

The supporting AI stack separates the gateway, vision, retrieval, knowledge graph, and response services. Pydantic schemas give them a common language for image inputs, location, citations, warnings, and errors, so mobile requests can move through the pipeline predictably.
Retrieval with a purpose

Image analysis feeds material-related searches and reuse suggestions. The knowledge graph connects materials to product ideas and relationships, while retrieved documents provide supporting information. Similarity scores rank candidates; they are not calibrated probabilities that an idea will work.
Useful under partial failure

The orchestrator assembles results from several services and reports partial responses explicitly. A local lexical search can stand in when vector retrieval is unavailable. Missing required model checkpoints fail closed, making an unavailable capability visible instead of silently inventing an answer.
technical.footnote: These details describe the supporting AI repository, which reports staging readiness. They are separate from the released app’s download figures.

title: Beyond the heat map
subtitle: The hottest neighborhood is only part of the story.
summary: Remote sensing and interpretable machine learning to study urban heat vulnerability across Phoenix.
intro: A surface-temperature map tells us where a city is hot. It does not, by itself, tell us which neighborhoods are most vulnerable. My research brought environmental and demographic information together to examine that difference.
facts: top-priority tracts shared by both rankings
sections: A different way to ask the question

I studied 369 Phoenix census tracts using Landsat imagery, land-cover indicators, and census demographics. Rather than treating temperature as the whole problem, I compared temperature-only priorities with a multidimensional view of neighborhood vulnerability.
When the rankings diverge

Only 17 of the 37 highest-priority tracts appeared in both rankings. That difference matters: a decision based only on surface heat can identify a substantially different set of neighborhoods from a decision that also considers their wider vulnerability.
Making the patterns interpretable

Clustering identified three vulnerability profiles, providing a way to discuss why neighborhoods differ and how cooling interventions might respond. The work connects remote sensing with the practical question of where—and on what basis—a city should focus its attention.
note: Paper: “Remote Sensing and Interpretable Machine Learning for Neighborhood-Level Urban Heat Vulnerability in Phoenix, Arizona.” Submitted and accepted by my supervising professor; unpublished. The graphic above illustrates the reported ranking overlap, not geographic boundaries.

technical.heading: One city. Three ways to read it.
modules: Environmental evidence

Landsat surface-temperature information and land-cover indicators describe the physical environment. The census tract is the neighborhood-scale unit of comparison, allowing environmental patterns and demographic information to be considered across the same 369 areas.
A change in the decision rule

I compared a temperature-only ranking with a multidimensional vulnerability ranking. Examining which tracts enter the top 37 makes the practical consequence visible: the definition of priority changes the places a cooling program would consider first.
Profiles that explain differences

Clustering identified three vulnerability profiles. These groupings give the analysis another layer beyond a ranked list: they help explain how neighborhoods differ and why one uniform intervention may not address every pattern of vulnerability.
technical.footnote: Surface temperature, demographic vulnerability, and intervention priority answer related but different questions. The study compares those perspectives; it does not measure the effects of a completed cooling program.

title: ZenithSync Assay Planner
subtitle: What should an experiment measure next?
organization: AI4S Open Innovation: AI for Life Science
summary: A Gaussian-process tool for choosing informative treatment and control measurements in organoid experiments.
intro: Every measurement uses part of an experiment’s budget. I built a planner that considers what is already known, where uncertainty remains, and how a shared control affects several treatment measurements at once.
sections: The shared-control problem

A treatment response often depends on a measured control. When several responses share that reference, their errors are related. The planner retains this dependence instead of treating the control as perfectly known, and considers purchasing additional control measurements alongside treatment wells.
Choosing a batch

A Gaussian process models response contrasts and their uncertainty. A finite-pool optimizer then selects a batch of wells to reduce average model uncertainty across the planned doses. I connected this method to a local browser interface, a command-line workflow, and traceable processing of public data.
Testing the claim

The frozen retrospective confirmation covered 6,496 paired assay contexts representing 100 patient IDs. Exact selection reduced mean squared prediction error by 32.82% versus random selection under the same model. Against the stronger greedy baseline, the improvement was 0.66%—an important limit on the size of the advantage.
note: These are retrospective research results. Prospective laboratory savings, clinical benefit, and transfer to perfused organ-on-a-chip experiments have not been demonstrated.

technical.heading: The control well is part of the model.
modules: Keep the covariance

Subtracting the same measured control from several treatment readings introduces shared error. With independent raw errors of variance s², the contrast-noise covariance is R = s²(I + 11ᵀ): 2s² on the diagonal and s² off it. The joint Gaussian model preserves that dependence.
Search the finite design space

The optimizer chooses a fixed-budget batch by reducing average posterior variance over target doses. Verified exchangeable wells can be grouped, allowing one representative per group-count pattern. This reduces enumeration without changing the optimum of the bounded problem.
Freeze, then evaluate

Model choices were fixed before confirmation on a separate public organoid study. Exact, greedy, and random policies share the same prediction model and measurement budget; patient-grouped analysis separates repeated assay contexts from independent patient IDs.
technical.footnote: The covariance objective depends on the design and observed-well locations, not the response values. This is a fixed-model batch design; predictions update with measurements, but the selection rule is not response-adaptive.
source: Read the mathematical and contribution audit

title: CollegeAdvisor
subtitle: An answer should come with a source.
summary: A college-advising application built around retrieval, citations, and knowing when information is insufficient.
intro: Admissions, financial aid, and transfer pathways all depend on specific information. At Athena AI Labs, I worked on an application that retrieves supporting material before constructing an answer, with checks for questions the available sources cannot support.
sections: Connecting the whole application

I developed a SwiftUI interface, a Python API, and retrieval-augmented generation workflows for college-advising questions. Student-profile integration supported personalized recommendations, while document ingestion organized the information the system could consult.
Retrieval before generation

The published architecture combines keyword and vector retrieval, source-authority weighting, specialized question handling, and a cite-or-abstain check. Its language model formats the response; retrieved evidence supplies the factual basis. The distinction helps make the answer’s support inspectable.
Making the work inspectable

I published CollegeAdvisor-RAG on Hugging Face with architecture notes and usage instructions. A model listing is also available on Kaggle. The portfolio focuses on the implemented retrieval and citation design; benchmark claims in a model card should not be read as a guarantee for every admissions question.
note: The diagram is a simplified presentation of the published architecture. The Hugging Face release is a documented model artifact, not a hosted advisory service.

technical.heading: Retrieval does the factual work.
modules: Two routes to the evidence

BM25 keyword retrieval captures exact names and terms, while dense retrieval finds passages with related meaning. Five ChromaDB collections organize the knowledge base. Combining these routes helps match both a specific college name and a less precisely worded question.
Check the question and the source

Source-authority weighting and specialized question handlers guide how retrieved material is used. A cite-or-abstain check keeps insufficient evidence visible rather than forcing every question into a confident answer. Student context enters through the application and API.
A smaller model, a narrower job

The published architecture uses a LoRA-adapted TinyLlama 1.1B model for response formatting. The retrieved evidence supplies factual content. Keeping those responsibilities separate makes it easier to inspect whether an answer is supported by its citations.
technical.footnote: Architecture details follow the published model card. They describe the system’s design, not a guarantee that every retrieved fact is current or every answer is correct.

title: Language in motion
subtitle: Studying the distance between words and signing.
summary: A language-to-motion research project spanning 3D reconstruction, learned motion codes, and the challenge of evaluating generated signing.
intro: Making science education more accessible led me to a difficult research question: how can language connect to coordinated movement? Sign-Translator explores that question while keeping generated motion distinct from linguistically validated American Sign Language.
sections: More than a sequence of hand poses

Signing coordinates the hands, body, face, gaze, and timing. I’m exploring how to represent those channels together, connect them to language, and carry the result into an articulated avatar. Each stage presents a different problem: recovering motion, learning its structure, and checking what a generated sequence actually communicates.
From a synthetic baseline to continuous motion

The initial runnable system connects a spatiotemporal graph network, a language–motion contrastive objective, and conditional diffusion on synthetic motion. The newer branch works with continuous video-derived motion and part-wise discrete codes. Keeping those experiments distinct makes it possible to compare methods without treating a system diagram as evidence that every component is complete.
When a better loss produced less movement

One continuous diffusion experiment reached a promising denoising loss while producing nearly static motion. Adding a velocity loss did not resolve the collapse. That result pushed the experiments toward discrete motion tokens and more direct checks of body, hand, and head dynamics—a reminder that the training objective and the behavior we care about can diverge.
note: Active research prototype. The diagrams document different parts of the research design, and the avatar image is a rig test. Neither generated movement nor a rendering check establishes linguistically valid ASL. Independent intelligibility evaluation remains necessary.

technical.heading: Language has to survive the whole pipeline.
modules: Put the motion on one clock

The continuous-data branch aligns front and side How2Sign video using landmark motion, then calibrates the cameras, triangulates positions, and fits joint rotations. Reprojection and rigid-bone checks constrain the reconstruction. These are video-derived estimates, with provenance retained, rather than motion-capture ground truth.
Learn a vocabulary of movement

A part-wise residual vector quantizer represents body, left hand, right hand, and face motion with discrete codes. The selected continuous-generation experiment predicts these codes from text plus spatial-locus conditioning. Separate channels preserve distinctions that a single stream of hand coordinates would miss.
Test what the score is measuring

An earlier retrieval evaluator scored motion with zeroed rotations surprisingly well: clip duration was leaking the answer. Fixed two-second windows, randomized offsets, and a duration-only control made that shortcut testable. A useful metric must respond to motion content, not just clip length.
technical.footnote: The continuous training experiments extend the original synthetic baseline. Generated motion still requires independent linguistic evaluation before it can support a claim of understandable ASL.

title: Science, clearly told
subtitle: From a biological idea to a story people can follow.
summary: Website development and entrepreneurship work for an iGEM Gold Medal synthetic biology team.
intro: A scientific project needs a clear explanation of what it does, how it works, and where it might be useful. For LCG-China, I led the wiki and entrepreneurship work that connected our team’s research with that wider story.
sections: Giving the research a structure

I directed the team’s website presentation, organizing scientific and business material into accessible explanations of the project, methods, and findings. The wiki gave different parts of the work a shared structure so readers could follow the reasoning as well as the results.
Thinking beyond the laboratory

I led development of the ExploreAid business plan for a proposed bacterial-cellulose bandage. The work considered customer needs, competing products, market positioning, production costs, and commercialization risks.
A team achievement
LCG-China earned an iGEM Gold Medal in 2024. My contribution focused on wiki development, entrepreneurship, and communicating the team’s scientific work to a wider audience.
note: ExploreAid was a proposed product and business plan; the team medal does not imply clinical validation or commercial release.

title: Finding a heading
subtitle: Software that has to answer to the wind.
summary: Control and simulation improvements for an autonomous sailboat navigating changing conditions.
intro: An autonomous boat has to turn imperfect information into a physical decision. My contributions to Kehillah Sailbot focused on navigation, steering, wind filtering, state estimation, and the simulator used to study the boat’s behavior.
sections: Closing the loop

A navigation decision is only useful if the boat can follow it. I contributed to the software that connects estimated conditions with steering behavior, including filtering wind information and improving the state estimates used by the controller.
Respecting physical constraints

My work included model-predictive steering with constraints on rudder movement. Explicit movement limits let the controller reason about actions the mechanism can perform, rather than assuming it can instantly reach any desired position.
Learning in simulation

I also contributed to the physics simulator and control improvements for evaluating boat behavior. Simulation provides a way to examine how changes in navigation and steering affect the system before drawing conclusions about performance on the water.
note: The illustration is conceptual. This page describes software contributions and does not report unverified competition or on-water performance.

technical.heading: A decision becomes a rudder angle.
modules: Connect the control loop

The team’s ROS 2 architecture separates sensor input, navigation, and actuation. GPS fixes and wind direction feed the control system, while rudder and sail commands travel on dedicated topics. That separation makes the data entering a decision and the command leaving it inspectable.
Constrain the next move

My model-predictive steering work included limits on rudder movement. A controller must choose from actions the mechanism can perform over time. State estimation and wind filtering improve the information used to make those choices under changing conditions.
Study behavior before deployment

The physics simulator provides a setting for examining navigation and control changes together. It connects the software question—what command should be issued?—with the physical question of how the boat responds. On-water performance remains a separate evaluation.
technical.footnote: The repository documents the team’s ROS 2 system. My contributions focus on navigation, steering, wind filtering, state estimation, and simulation.

title: A better test for an agent
subtitle: Making software experiments easier to trust.
summary: Repository-task evaluation and training-data tools for studying a coding agent’s behavior.
intro: Before asking whether a coding agent improved, it helps to know exactly what it was tested on. This project focuses on the infrastructure behind that question: task provenance, evaluation isolation, deterministic training schedules, and recoverable runs.
sections: Knowing where each task came from

I developed source tracking and training-data preparation tools for repository tasks, alongside checks for overlap between development and evaluation data. These checks help prevent an apparent improvement from coming from exposure to the evaluation material.
Making runs comparable

Deterministic schedules, token accounting, and recovery checks make the conditions of a run explicit. Test-result validation adds another boundary: the evaluation needs to check the intended behavior and preserve enough information to inspect failures.
Separating infrastructure from performance

The project was developed around the Gemma developer-agent competition. The public repository documents implementation and readiness limits. Evaluation tooling and successful software tests do not, by themselves, demonstrate learned gains on unseen repository tasks.
note: Research tooling in development. The project does not yet establish learned performance gains on unseen repository tasks.

technical.heading: Make an improvement reproducible.
modules: Track the task’s lineage

Repository tasks carry source provenance and evaluation contracts. Checks for overlap and quarantine keep questionable material out of the training path. This makes the boundary between development data and held-out evaluation something the tooling can inspect.
Read the tests, not just the headline

The JUnit audit preserves individual test-case outcomes and rejects contradictory aggregate counts. Failures, errors, and skipped cases remain distinct. A successful process exit or an attractive summary count cannot substitute for the underlying test evidence.
Resume the same experiment

Deterministic schedules and token accounting make training inputs and update boundaries explicit. Resume checks reconstruct the remaining schedule and reject corrupted counters, helping a recovered run continue the intended experiment rather than quietly becoming a different one.
technical.footnote: These are implemented evaluation and training-preparation mechanisms. The repository does not yet establish learned gains on unseen repository tasks.
